about: Every source of the titration lab's record (docs/research/phase-3/titration.json) and of its primer (src/chem-data/titration/primer.ts), each fetched and read on the retrieval date, or on the later date its own citation gives. A source with `file` has its copy in this folder, as downloaded, with the sha256 of that copy; a source with none was read and no copy is kept. `fetchedSha256`, on a source with no copy, is the sha256 of the page as it was fetched on the day it was read, or, for a page that a script draws (the sheets whose ids begin `flinn-sds-`), of the text the page showed in a browser that day: a record of which page that was, not the hash of any file here, and nothing checks it. Each `supports` row names one stored value by its path in the record, gives in `prints` the figure or label exactly as the source prints it, and says in `where`, in this project's words, where it is. A row whose field is `primer` marks a source the primer rests on: its `prints` is a title or a heading as the source prints it, and which passage a paragraph rests on, and what that passage establishes, is said in the paragraph's support line in the primer. The statements of all three bottles are those of one supplier's safety data sheets, read and not kept: the sheet for concentrated hydrochloric acid, and the sheets for sodium hydroxide and for phenolphthalein themselves, the solids. The owner asked for this supplier's sheets as the lab's reference for hazards. The note under the acid's statements and the note under the base's rest on the same supplier's sheets for solutions of the strength on the bench, two for the acid and one for the base; the note under the indicator's rests on another supplier's sheet, for a solution of the strength and solvent the bottle is taken to be, because the first supplier's sheet for a phenolphthalein solution is for one in alcohol alone. No bottle has a `reference`: the rows of each sheet give what it prints, and those of `flinn-sds-395` say in which form the statements are stored and why. README.md in this folder gives the attribution the two Wikipedia copies require.

sources.citation: Tamura, Z.; Abe, S.; Ito, K.; Maeda, M. Spectrophotometric Analysis of the Relationship between Dissociation and Coloration, and of the Structural Formulas of Phenolphthalein in Aqueous Solution. Anal. Sci. 1996, 12 (6), 927-930. https://doi.org/10.2116/analsci.12.927 (read as the publisher's PDF on J-STAGE, linked here; retrieved 2026-10-04).

supports.where: The abstract, and the results on page 929: the first of phenolphthalein's two acid constants, estimated from absorption spectra measured in 0.2 M phosphate buffers at 25 ± 2 °C.

The same two places: the second acid constant. The abstract says that only the form that has lost both protons is coloured, and gives a third constant of 12 for the slow fading in strong base, which the model leaves out.

supports.where: Table 3, the first row (liquid water at 0.1 MPa below 100 °C), the column for 25 °C: the release's pK_w. Section 3 says the model takes the ions on the molal standard state.

Table 2, the release's own test value at 300 K and a density of 1.0 g/cm³. The equations (2) to (4), written out with the parameters of Table 1, were checked against it before being worked at 298.15 K and 0.99705 g/cm³, where they give 13.994.

sources.citation: Perrin, D. D., Ed. Ionisation Constants of Inorganic Acids and Bases in Aqueous Solution, 2nd ed.; IUPAC Chemical Data Series 29; Pergamon: Oxford, 1982. The book was not read: the two constants were taken from a secondary transcription, Wikipedia's article Carbonic acid, revision 1376246456 of 2026-09-23, linked here, whose infobox cites the book's entry for carbonic acid (retrieved 2026-10-04).

supports.where: The infobox's acidity line, the second of its three figures, the one marked hydrous, with no temperature beside it. The first figure, 3.75, is marked anhydrous and 25 °C and is not the one the model uses. The page's section on bicarbonate and carbonate prints 6.35 again for this constant, and before it 6.77, worked out for 25 °C and a solution with no other ions.

The same line of the infobox, its third figure, with no temperature beside it: the second constant. The page's section on bicarbonate and carbonate prints 9.93 for this constant, worked out for 25 °C and a solution with no other ions. Beside its second 6.35 the same section prints a difference of 3.49 and cites for it Pines et al., J. Phys. Chem. B 2016, 120, 2440, a paper this project did not read; the difference is not taken as a value of this constant and nothing is worked from it.

sources.citation: U.S. Geological Survey. PHREEQC version 3, release 3.8.6-17100: the database file database/phreeqc.dat in the archive phreeqc-3.8.6-17100.tar.gz, which the page linked here lists; read and not kept (retrieved 2026-10-05). A copy of the file on GitHub (https://github.com/usgs-coupled/phreeqc3, database/phreeqc.dat at commit b0b3be7), fetched the same day, prints the same two figures. That a log_k in such a file is the constant at 25 °C is the definition in the program's manual: Parkhurst, D. L.; Appelo, C. A. J. Description of Input and Examples for PHREEQC Version 3; U.S. Geological Survey Techniques and Methods, book 6, chapter A43; 2013; the entry for SOLUTION_SPECIES (https://water.usgs.gov/water-resources/software/PHREEQC/documentation/phreeqc3-html/phreeqc3-50.htm, read the same day).

supports.where: Under SOLUTION_SPECIES, the log_k line of the reaction in which carbonate takes up two hydrogen ions and gives dissolved carbon dioxide and water (line 241 of the file): the constant at 25 °C, by the manual's definition of log_k. The first constant with dissolved carbon dioxide as the acid is this figure less the 10.329 of the reaction before it, 6.352, which is worked out in the note and not printed in the file.

Under SOLUTION_SPECIES, the log_k line of the reaction in which carbonate takes up one hydrogen ion and gives bicarbonate (line 234 of the file): the constant at 25 °C, taken from the 16.681 to give the first constant.
The same line: read the other way, bicarbonate giving up its hydrogen ion, it is the second constant at 25 °C.

sources.citation: Flinn Scientific, Inc. Safety Data Sheet: Hydrochloric Acid 6 M - 12 M (Concentrated), SDS number sds_395; revision date December 3, 2018 (read on 2026-10-05; no copy is kept).

supports.where: The sheet's title, after the words Hydrochloric Acid: the strengths the sheet is for. The heading over the bottle's statements gives them as 6 M to 12 M.

Section 3, the concentration column, in the row for hydrochloric acid, the rest being water: the composition the sheet gives for the solution its title names. The sheet does not say on what basis the percentage is.
Under the title, after the words Revision Date, and again at the foot of the sheet: the revision that was read. The sheet does not say which rule its classification is made under.
Under the title, after the words Signal Word. The sheet prints it in capitals; the record stores Danger, the form its schema has for the word.

supports.prints: Causes severe skin and eye burns and damage (H314+H318)
supports.where: Section 2, the first of the three hazard classes it lists: category 1, for corrosion or irritation of the skin and damage to the eyes. The sheet prints each statement and then its code or codes in brackets, and where it pairs two codes it joins them with a plus sign and gives the pair one statement in wording of its own. The record stores the sheet's own three lines, each with its codes in front as printed, then a colon and the statement, and not one line for each code in the GHS's standard wording for that code: the sheet does not print that wording, and a line for each code would put under this source words that are not in it.
Section 2, the second of the three: category 4, for acute toxicity by mouth and by breathing in. The two codes are stored in the order the sheet prints them.

Section 2, the last of the three: category 1, for corrosion of metals. The section prints no other hazard code, and so not H331, which the build refuses on this bottle. After the three classes it has one more sentence, on a cancer listing for mists of the acid in industry: that sentence carries no hazard code, is not a GHS hazard statement, and is not carried into the record. Nor are the precautionary statements the section prints beside two of the classes, whose codes begin with P.

supports.where: The sheet's title, after the words Hydrochloric Acid Solution: the strengths the sheet is for. By this title the 51 values of the bottle's label from 0.1000 to 0.1050 M are under this sheet, and the 150 below them under the sheet for less than 0.1 M (`flinn-sds-395.3`). The note rests on both, and says that the acid is handled as this one, the stricter, says: that is the owner's decision of 2026-10-05.
Under the title, after the words Revision Date, and again at the foot of the sheet: the revision that was read. The sheet does not say which rule its classification is made under.

supports.prints: Causes severe skin burns and eye damage (H314)
supports.where: Section 2, the first of the three hazard classes it lists: category 1, for corrosion or irritation of the skin. The note gives the code and says the statement in the project's words.
Section 2, the second of the three: category 3, for toxicity to one organ after a single exposure, here irritation of the airways.

Section 2, the last of the three: category 5, for acute toxicity by mouth. The section prints no other hazard code. It prints one precautionary statement, whose code begins with P, and after the three classes the sentence on a cancer listing for mists of the acid in industry that the sheet for concentrated acid has: neither of those is a GHS hazard statement, and they are not carried into the record.

Section 3, the concentration column, in the row for hydrochloric acid, the rest being water. The sheet does not say on what basis the percentage is. Taken by mass, 2% is about 0.55 mol/L (worked out as the note's 0.4% is), so the table starts well above the 0.1 M of the sheet's own title, and above every value of this bottle's label. The note follows the titles, which put the label on both sides of the line between the two sheets, and does not use this figure.
Section 8: the precautionary statement that calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.
Sections 7 and 8: the precautionary statement that the acid is used only in a hood or where the air is well changed.

Section 4, under the eyes: they are rinsed with water for several minutes, contact lenses are taken out if they are worn and come out easily, and the rinsing is kept up after that. The sheet gives no number of minutes.

Section 4, straight after the codes for the eyes: a poison centre or a doctor is to be called at once. The same section says that after contact with the skin or the hair the clothing that was wetted is taken off at once and the skin rinsed with water.
